:::{#exm-matmul-zero-divisors}
#### A product of two nonzero matrices can be the zero matrix

With

$$
\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\matr{B} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix},
$$

neither matrix is the zero matrix (@def-zero-matrix), but

$$
\begin{aligned}
\matr{A}\matr{B}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 & 1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 1 \\ 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 & 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 1 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \matr{0}_{2 \times 2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For numbers, $ab = 0$ forces $a = 0$ or $b = 0$.
For matrices it does not.

Because $\matr{A}\matr{0}_{2 \times 2} = \matr{0}_{2 \times 2} = \matr{A}\matr{B}$
while $\matr{B} \neq \matr{0}_{2 \times 2}$,
the factor $\matr{A}$ cannot be cancelled from $\matr{A}\matr{B} = \matr{A}\matr{0}_{2 \times 2}$.
This does not contradict @thm-invertible-cancel,
because $\matr{A}$ is singular:
its second row is zero, so $\matr{A}\matr{C}$ has a zero second row for every $2 \times 2$ matrix $\matr{C}$,
and $\matr{A}\matr{C}$ can never be $\matr{I}_2$.

:::
